definition: Semantic computing is a field of computing that combines elements of semantic analysis, natural language processing, data mining, knowledge graphs, and related fields.
details: Semantic computing addresses three core problems: Understanding the (possibly naturally-expressed) intentions (semantics) of users and expressing them in a machine-processable format Understanding the meanings (semantics) of computational content (of various sorts, including, but is not limited to, text, video, audio, process, network, software and hardware) and expressing them in a machine-processable format Mapping the semantics of user with that of content for the purpose of content retrieval, management, creation, etc. The IEEE has held an International Conference on Semantic Computing since 2007. A conference on Knowledge Graphs and Semantic Computing has been held since 2015.

explainer.lead: Semantic computing treats meaning itself as the thing to be captured and manipulated, rather than just surface strings or bytes. It matters because it links what a user intends to what content actually says, which is the core problem behind search, retrieval and assistants.

tiers.eli5: Instead of matching words on a page, it tries to understand what you mean and what the page means, then connects the two.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to build pipelines that convert user requests and content (text, video, audio, process, network, software, hardware) into machine-processable semantic representations, then map one to the other for retrieval. A common pitfall is mismatched representations between the user side and the content side, which silently breaks the mapping.
tiers.paperLevel: Semantic computing combines semantic analysis, natural language processing, data mining and knowledge graphs, and addresses three problems: understanding user intentions and expressing them in machine-processable form, understanding the meanings of computational content and expressing them likewise, and mapping user semantics to content semantics for retrieval. It is a field rather than a single formula, so it has no single formal limit.

explainer.example: A user asks a loosely worded question; the system converts the intent into a machine-processable representation, converts candidate documents and media into semantic representations, and retrieves items whose semantics map to the request.
